body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Accuracy of a month-3 transition self-rating for predicting first-year separation among new graduate nurses","authors":"Adebayo-Lund K, Moreau-Singh T, Halvorsen-Oyelaran J","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Nursing Workforce Studies","doi":"10.5555/jnws.2022.0213","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Background: early identification of new graduate nurses at risk of leaving could focus retention support. Methods: in two teaching hospitals, 412 residents completed a 15-item transition self-rating at month 3, and separation from the employing hospital within 12 months of hire was taken from human resources records by staff blind to the scores. Results: 79 residents (19 percent) separated. At a score of 30 or below, sensitivity was 0.71 (95 percent CI 0.60 to 0.81) and specificity 0.68 (0.63 to 0.73); the area under the ROC curve was 0.74. Positive predictive value was 0.35 at the observed prevalence. Conclusions: the self-rating identified most nurses who later left but flagged many who stayed, and the threshold should be validated locally before use."},{"title":"Transition shock in the first year of practice: validation of a 15-item self-rating scale for new graduate nurses","authors":"Okafor-Brennan M, Sato-Lindqvist A","year":2019,"venue":"Transition to Practice Review","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined the measurement properties of a 15-item self-rating of transition difficulty completed by 638 new graduate nurses in five hospitals. Items cover workload, clinical confidence, belonging and preceptor support, scored 0 to 4 and summed to 0 to 60. Internal consistency was high (Cronbach alpha 0.88) and a four-factor structure fitted the data acceptably. Test-retest reliability over two weeks was 0.81 in a subsample of 94 nurses. Scores were lowest between months 3 and 4 of practice and rose thereafter. The scale was not evaluated against later turnover, and the authors caution that it measures experienced difficulty rather than intention to leave."},{"title":"Nurse residency programmes and first-year retention of new graduate nurses: a systematic review","authors":"Castillo-Hartmann R, Nwachukwu-Berg L, Fairweather-Iqbal S","year":2021,"venue":"Nursing Retention Quarterly","doi":"10.5555/nrq.2021.0077","providerType":"review","abstract":"We searched four bibliographic databases to 2020 for studies reporting 12-month retention of new graduate nurses with and without a structured residency programme. Twenty-four studies met the criteria, 21 of them before-after comparisons within single organisations. Reported 12-month retention ranged from 78 to 94 percent with a residency and from 64 to 88 percent without. Programme content, length and the definition of retention varied widely, and nine studies counted internal transfers as losses. No included study evaluated a screening step to target extra support. Certainty was low because of uncontrolled designs and inconsistent outcome definitions."},{"title":"Stated intention to leave and actual separation among early-career nurses: a 12-month follow-up","authors":"Petrovic-Amadi D, Lindgren-Oduya H","year":2017,"venue":"Clinical Staff Development Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Intention to leave is often used as a stand-in for turnover. We asked 355 nurses in their first two years of practice at six months whether they intended to leave their employer within a year, and followed actual separation in human resources records. Sixty-two nurses (17 percent) separated. Stated intention identified 30 of them (sensitivity 0.48) and was absent in 253 of the 293 who stayed (specificity 0.86). Nurses who left for family or relocation reasons rarely reported an intention in advance. The authors conclude that stated intention misses about half of later leavers and should not be the only trigger for retention support."},{"title":"Human resources records as the reference standard for nurse turnover research: completeness and misclassification of separation data","authors":"Whitcombe-Adeyemi F, Tanaka-Riordan P, Bello-Sorensen C","year":2020,"venue":"Journal of Nursing Workforce Studies","doi":"10.5555/jnws.2020.0048","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared human resources separation records for 1,904 nurses in three hospitals with payroll end dates and manager confirmation. Separation dates were present and correct for 99 percent of nurses who left. Reason codes were less reliable: 23 percent of separations coded as resignations were internal transfers to another unit or site of the same organisation, and 9 percent of retirements were coded as resignations. The authors recommend defining turnover as leaving the organisation, using dates rather than reason codes, and stating before analysis how internal transfers are handled."},{"title":"A targeted mentoring booster for new graduate nurses with low transition scores: a before-after evaluation","authors":"Kowalski-Mensah A, Duarte-Fitzgerald N","year":2024,"venue":"Nurse Education and Practice Reports","doi":"10.5555/nepr.2024.0130","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"One hospital offered six additional mentoring sessions to new graduate nurses who scored in the lowest quarter of a transition self-rating at month 3. Twelve-month retention of all residents was 81 percent in the two years before the booster and 88 percent in the two years after. Uptake among eligible residents was 64 percent. Other changes during the period included a new preceptor allowance and a regional hiring freeze, and the evaluation had no concurrent comparison group. The authors suggest that a screening threshold should be validated before a booster is tied to it."},{"title":"Prevalence of first-year separation and the stability of screening thresholds across hospitals","authors":"Iwu-Castellano B, Ferreira-Nakamura O, Holm-Achterberg V","year":2016,"venue":"Transition to Practice Review","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using transition ratings and human resources data from 11 hospitals, we examined how the usefulness of a fixed screening threshold changed with local separation rates. First-year separation ranged from 12 to 27 percent between hospitals. Sensitivity and specificity at a fixed threshold varied little, but the positive predictive value ranged from 0.21 at 12 percent separation to 0.44 at 27 percent. Two hospitals whose residency seminars were held later in the first year showed lower sensitivity. The authors recommend reporting predictive values at the local prevalence and fixing the timing of the rating."}]}
